items.title: RNet: Users pay for their own AI usage instead of apps covering token costs
items.raw_excerpt:
Developers currently pay for AI usage and then recover costs through subscriptions, rate limits, or pricing tiers. This creates a few problems: 1.Apps have to track per-user usage and build complex billing logic. 2.Users end up paying multiple times for the same underlying AI across different apps. I’m experimenting with a different model: users fund their own AI usage directly, similar to prepaid mobile data. In this system: 1.Users preload a balance
2.Each request is signed by the user
3.The cost is deducted from the user’s balance per request
4.Apps don’t pay for tokens or manage billing I built a prototype called rNet. The protocol is live, with client libraries available (npm, Maven), and the docs are open:
https://www.rnetai.org/ This is still early, and I’m mainly looking for feedba

excerpt_i18n.en: At the Google Cloud Next conference in Las Vegas, Google Senior Vice President Amin Vahdat unveiled not one but two chips: the TPU 8t and TPU 8i. This marks the first clear "split" in the history of Google's TPU family—one chip dedicated to training, the other to inference. "With the rise of AI agents, we believe the community will benefit from chips optimized separately for training and serving needs," Amin Vahdat wrote in an official blog post. Google has sent a clear signal: the era of relying solely on NVIDIA's "universal chips" in a rough-and-tumble manner is over, giving way to a "fine-grained division of labor" akin to an assembly line. The core focus of this split is the TPU 8i, designed for "running," and the impending "Agentic AI" era it represents. Why split the TPU? The answer is simple: efficiency. Training and inference may both involve AI computing, but they are fundamentally different. Training is like a top student devouring an entire human library, pursuing "brute force to create miracles" to refine model capabilities. Inference, on the other hand, is like that same student working as a customer service rep at a big company—no longer about who knows the most, but who responds fastest, costs least, and offers the best value. In the past, the industry defaulted to a single chip handling both training and inference because AI was still in its early computational stages: models weren't as large, and scenarios weren't as numerous.
excerpt_i18n.es: En la conferencia Google Cloud Next en Las Vegas, el vicepresidente sénior de Google, Amin Vahdat, no mostró un solo chip, sino dos: TPU 8t y TPU 8i. Es la primera vez en la historia de la familia TPU de Google que se produce una "separación" clara: uno está diseñado para entrenamiento y el otro para inferencia. "Con el auge de los agentes de IA, creemos que la comunidad se beneficiará de chips optimizados por separado para las necesidades de entrenamiento y servicio", escribió Amin Vahdat en el blog oficial. items.title: 对话清华商宇丨从生成视频到支撑行动，世界模型需要新的评测标准
items.raw_excerpt: 在今天的 AI 叙事里，“世界模型”几乎成了通往具身智能的必经之路。 它被期待理解物理规律、预测环境变化，并为机器人决策提供依据。但一个尖锐的问题是：当一个模型能生成一段足够逼真的未来视频时，我们究竟该相信它真的理解了世界，还是只是更擅长复刻世界的表象？ 咬了一口的苹果会自动愈合，坠落的杯子在空中漂移——在具身智能的视角下，这种AI视频“感知与功能的断裂”无疑是致命的。 一个模型即便能生成 4K 分辨率的视觉幻象，如果它无法理解重力约束、因果关联与物体永久性，它就永远无法支撑机器人在复杂物理世界中的抓取、规划与交互。视觉真实不等于功能可用，这道长期被忽视的“裂缝”，正是当前视觉智能通往 AGI 的最大障碍。 CVPR 2026 正在释放一个明确的信号：计算机视觉（CV）与计算机图形学（CG）的传统边界正在模糊。视觉研究的主线正从单纯的“像素预测”转向对“世界动力学”的重建，世界模型不再仅仅满足于“看”，而是要构建一个具备物理一致性的内部沙盒。这意味着，下一代视觉智能必须跨越 2D 藩篱，去硬碰硬地解决因果律、重力与 3D 空间的拓扑逻辑。 这种转向，不仅标志着视觉研究正在从“图像处理”回归到“世界建模”，更核心的演进在于，世界模型正从“被动观测”转向“动作驱动”。 作为 CVPR 2026 备受瞩目的竞赛项目，清华团队提出的 WorldArena 恰逢其时。在论文《WorldArena: A Unified Benchmark for Evaluating Perception and Functional Utility of Embodied World Models》中，它审问的是模型作为“具身大脑”的真实含金量：能否作为可靠的数据引擎？能否充当精准的策略评估环境？能否在长程任务中保持逻辑的不漂移？ 它将会对过去世界模型评测沿用视频生成的逻辑——画面是否清晰、运动是否

excerpt_i18n.en: In today’s AI narrative, the “world model” has become almost a necessary path to embodied intelligence. It is expected to understand physical laws, predict environmental changes, and provide a basis for robot decision-making. But a sharp question arises: when a model can generate a sufficiently realistic future video, should we believe it truly understands the world, or is it merely better at replicating the surface of reality? A bitten apple heals on its own, a falling cup drifts in midair—from the perspective of embodied intelligence, this “disconnect between perception and function” in AI videos is undoubtedly fatal. Even if a model can generate 4K-resolution visual illusions, if it cannot grasp gravity constraints, causal relationships, and object permanence, it will never support a robot’s grasping, planning, and interaction in the complex physical world. Visual realism does not equal functional usability—this long-overlooked “crack” is the biggest obstacle on the path from current visual intelligence to AGI. CVPR 2026 is sending a clear signal: the traditional boundary between computer vision (CV) and computer graphics (CG) is blurring. The main thread of vision research is shifting from mere “pixel prediction” to the reconstruction of “world dynamics.” World models are no longer content with just “seeing”; they aim to build an internal sandbox with physical consistency. This means that next-generation visual intelligence must break through the 2D barrier and directly tackle causality, gravity, and the topological logic of 3D space. Se espera que comprenda las leyes físicas, prediga cambios en el entorno y proporcione fundamentos para la toma de decisiones de los robots. Pero surge una pregunta contundente: cuando un modelo puede generar un video futuro lo suficientemente realista, ¿debemos creer que realmente entiende el mundo, o simplemente es más hábil replicando su apariencia? Una manzana mordida se recompone sola, una taza que cae flota en el aire —desde la perspectiva de la inteligencia encarnada, esta "ruptura entre percepción y función" en los videos de IA es sin duda letal. excerpt_i18n.en: In recent years, video generation technology has achieved remarkable progress. From diffusion model-based approaches to large-scale video foundation models, the visual quality of generated results has gradually approached that of the real world. However, upon closer examination of these models, a more fundamental question emerges: are they truly "understanding the world," or merely "fitting pixel distributions"? Traditional video generation methods are mostly built upon 2D image space, synthesizing dynamic content through frame-by-frame modeling. While this paradigm excels in short time scales and visual performance, it also reveals a series of fundamental limitations: camera motion is difficult to control precisely, multi-object interactions lack consistency, long-term generation is prone to structural drift, and even basic physical laws are violated in complex scenes. The common root of these issues lies in the models' lack of the ability to model "the world itself." It is against this backdrop that the "World Model" has gradually become a core research direction in visual generation and intelligent systems. Unlike traditional methods, world models aim to construct an internal representation that can uniformly describe spatial structure, temporal evolution, and physical laws, enabling models not only to generate visual content but also to reason, predict, and even support decision-making. In a sense, this shift marks a transition in research goals from "generating results that look real" to "modeling a world that is fundamentally plausible." This paradigm evolution is unfolding across multiple dimensions simultaneously: at the representation level, moving from 2D pixels to 3D/4D geometry.
excerpt_i18n.es: En los últimos años, la tecnología de generación de video ha logrado avances notables. Desde métodos basados en modelos de difusión hasta modelos fundamentales de video a gran escala, los resultados generados se han ido acercando gradualmente al mundo real en términos de calidad visual. Sin embargo, al examinar más a fondo estos modelos, surge una pregunta más esencial: ¿están realmente "comprendiendo el mundo" o simplemente "ajustando la distribución de píxeles"? La mayoría de los métodos tradicionales de generación de video se basan en el espacio de imágenes 2D, sintetizando contenido dinámico mediante el modelado cuadro por cuadro. Aunque este paradigma muestra un buen rendimiento en escalas de tiempo cortas y en la representación visual, también revela una serie de limitaciones fundamentales: el movimiento de la cámara es difícil de controlar con precisión y la interacción entre múltiples objetos carece de coherencia.

excerpt_i18n.en: In 2025, AI computing power enters deep waters. On one hand, demand continues to spill over: the scale of large model training is still expanding, inference requests are growing exponentially, and investment in data centers shows no signs of cooling down. On the other hand, a series of hidden constraints are gradually surfacing—computing power utilization remains persistently low, system jitter occurs frequently, and cluster efficiency struggles to maintain stability. The industry is gradually realizing that the bottleneck does not always lie in "computing power" itself. In many cases, the problem is stuck in the "data" link. When the scale of computing clusters expands to tens of thousands of cards, any latency fluctuation in any link can be amplified into an overall performance issue. Some cloud service outages, on the surface, appear to be caused by scheduling algorithm failures, but the deeper reason is the mismatch between data supply and computing rhythm—data cannot be organized, moved, and distributed in time, leaving computing power idling in waiting. This brings a field long regarded as a basic component back into the core spotlight: storage. In the past, the task of storage was to solve "how to store it"; in the AI era, it begins to determine "how fast it computes." It is against this backdrop that "AI SSD" has emerged, and almost all mainstream storage vendors are trying to deliver their own answers. But the question follows—when the entire industry is making AI SSDs, what constitutes truly effective improvement? What exactly does storage need to change for AI?
